intro: Seven scenarios you have not seen, each with four quick questions. Read the scenario twice, answer, then read every explanation.
checklist: Read the scenario twice. Note who is deciding and who is affected.
Decide which level of government, branch or principle is involved before you look at the options.
Match a detail in the scenario to the idea it shows. Every correct answer points to a specific detail.
Rule out options that are true in general but not shown in this scenario.
readHint: Read the scenario twice before you answer. The explanation appears after each question.

sources.caption: Scenario 1. Is Tarvin a democracy?
sources.text: Tarvin holds an election every three years. At the last election eight parties stood, and an independent electoral commission counted the votes. Newspapers often criticise the government, and last year a court ruled against the government over a new mining law; the government accepted the ruling and rewrote the law. In March, however, Tarvin passed a law requiring a permit for any public protest. Since then, permits have been refused to every group that opposes the government, while groups that support it have been approved.

qs.q: Which detail is the strongest evidence that the rule of law operates in Tarvin?
o: The government accepted a court ruling against it and rewrote the law
Eight parties stood at the last election
Newspapers often criticise the government
Elections are held every three years
qs.x: The rule of law means everyone, including the government, must follow the law. Accepting a court's ruling against itself is the clearest sign of that. The other details show other democratic features.

qs.q: Which feature of democracy is most directly limited by the way protest permits are being decided?
o: Citizens' freedom to participate and express disagreement
Regular elections
An independent electoral commission
The separation of powers
qs.x: Protest is a form of participation and expression. Refusing permits only to opponents limits that freedom for one side of politics.

qs.q: Which conclusion about Tarvin is best supported by the whole scenario?
o: Tarvin has many democratic features, but its treatment of protests is undermining one of them
Tarvin is not a democracy because it has passed a law about protests
Tarvin is a complete democracy because it holds regular elections
Tarvin is not a democracy because a court ruled against the government
qs.x: Good conclusions weigh all the evidence. Most details show a working democracy. The permit refusals are a specific threat to one freedom, not proof that the whole system has failed.

qs.q: A newspaper wants to test whether the permit law is being applied unfairly. Which evidence would be most useful?
o: A list of every permit application, showing which were approved or refused and the reasons given
A speech by an opposition leader saying the law is unfair
An online poll of the newspaper's readers
A photograph of one large protest from several years ago
qs.x: Checkable records of every decision would show a pattern if there is one. Speeches, polls and old photographs show opinions or single moments, not how the law is being applied.

sources.caption: Scenario 2. One week in Canberra
sources.text: Monday: the House of Representatives passes a bill to raise the fine for littering on Commonwealth land. Tuesday: the Senate passes the same bill and the Governor-General gives it royal assent. Wednesday: the Department of the Environment puts up new signs and begins issuing fines. Thursday: a person who was fined argues in court that the sign was unreadable, and the magistrate decides the fine does not stand. Friday: a minister says publicly that the magistrate got it wrong, but accepts the decision.

qs.q: Which branch of government was at work on Monday and Tuesday?
o: The legislature
The executive
The judiciary
The electoral commission
qs.x: Parliament, meaning the House of Representatives and the Senate, makes and changes laws. That is the legislature. Royal assent is the final step of making a law.

qs.q: The department putting up signs and issuing fines is an example of which branch?
o: The executive, putting the law into action
The legislature, making the law
The judiciary, interpreting the law
The Opposition, scrutinising the law
qs.x: Government departments carry out and enforce laws under the direction of ministers. That is the executive.

qs.q: Why does Thursday's decision matter for the separation of powers?
o: It shows the courts decide independently how a law applies, even against the government
It shows judges can change the wording of laws passed by Parliament
It shows departments must ask a court before issuing any fine
It shows the Senate can overturn court decisions
qs.x: The judiciary interprets and applies laws independently. A court can rule that a fine was wrongly issued. It does not rewrite the law, and no other branch can direct its decision.

qs.q: What does the minister's response on Friday show?
o: Members of the executive can disagree with a court but must accept its decision
Ministers can overrule a magistrate if they disagree strongly
The judiciary must apologise when a minister disagrees
Court decisions apply only to ordinary citizens
qs.x: Disagreeing publicly is allowed. Refusing to obey is not. Accepting the decision shows the rule of law and an independent judiciary working together.

sources.caption: Scenario 3. The Wattle Street skate park
sources.text: A group of Year 8 students wants a skate park built on unused council land in Wattle Street. The council's draft budget for next year is open for public comment for four weeks. Residents can lodge a written submission, speak for three minutes at the next council meeting, or sign a petition at the local library. One student suggests spray-painting SKATE PARK NOW on the council office wall. Another has found a social-media post claiming the council secretly plans to sell the land, but the post gives no source.

qs.q: Why is the local council the right body to approach?
o: Local parks and recreation facilities on council land are council responsibilities
The federal government manages every park in Australia
Only state MPs can approve new buildings
Councils decide where schools are built
qs.x: Councils look after local land, parks and community facilities. Schools are a state responsibility, and the federal government does not run local parks.

qs.q: Which proposed action would be unlawful and likely to harm the campaign?
o: Spray-painting the council office wall
Speaking for three minutes at the council meeting
Lodging a written submission on the draft budget
Collecting signatures at the library
qs.x: Damaging property is a crime, not civic action. Lawful participation such as submissions, speaking at meetings and petitions is how citizens influence decisions in a democracy.

qs.q: What should the students do about the social-media post before using it?
o: Check it against a reliable source, such as council meeting minutes, before repeating it
Share it widely because it supports their cause
Quote it in their submission as proof the council cannot be trusted
Give up on the budget process because the land is already sold
qs.x: Civic action works best when it is accurate. An unsourced post could be wrong. Council minutes and reports can be checked.

qs.q: Which detail would make the students' submission most convincing to councillors?
o: Evidence such as the number of young people living nearby and the lack of other facilities in the area
A statement that everyone at their school loves skating
A promise to protest every week until the park is built
A list of the councillors they plan to vote against in future
qs.x: Decision-makers respond to evidence about need and community benefit. Threats and vague claims are easy to dismiss.

sources.caption: Scenario 4. The new phone rule
sources.text: A school introduces a rule: phones must be switched off and in lockers from 8:30 am until 3:15 pm, and a phone seen or heard in that time will be held at the office until the end of the day. The rule is emailed to every family, printed in the student planner and explained at assembly. It has not changed in two years. Some students argue the rule is unfair because they catch two buses to school and want to tell their parents when they are running late.

qs.q: Which characteristic of an effective law does the rule show most clearly?
o: It is clear and understood: it states exactly what is banned, when, and what happens
It reflects every student's values
It changes whenever students complain
It is enforced only when a teacher chooses to
qs.x: Precise times and a stated consequence leave no room for argument about what the rule means. Clarity makes a rule easier to follow and to enforce.

qs.q: Emailing families, printing the rule in the planner and explaining it at assembly make the rule...
o: known
stable
enforceable
popular
qs.x: A rule only works if the people it applies to know about it. The school has communicated it in three ways.

qs.q: The students who catch two buses are questioning which characteristic?
o: Whether the rule reflects the values and needs of the people it applies to
Whether the rule is stable
Whether the rule is clear
Whether the rule is known
qs.x: An effective law needs to reflect society's values and circumstances. The students are not confused about the rule. They argue it does not fit their needs.

qs.q: How is this school rule different from a law?
o: A law is made and enforced by legal authorities and breaking it has legal consequences; a school rule applies only within the school
A law is always written down and a rule never is
A rule applies to adults and a law applies to children
There is no difference, because all rules are laws
qs.x: Laws are formal rules made by Parliament or councils and enforced by police and courts. School rules apply only to that community and carry school consequences.

sources.caption: Scenario 5. Election night in Westhaven
sources.text: Westhaven is a fictional state. Its lower house has 88 seats. The results are in. Harbour Party 42 seats. Plains Party 38 seats. Rivers Alliance 5 seats. Independents 3 seats. Total 88.

qs.q: How many seats are needed for a majority government in Westhaven?
qs.x: A majority is more than half. Half of 88 is 44, so 45 seats are needed. Winning the most seats is not the same as winning a majority.

qs.q: Can the Harbour Party govern alone?
o: No. 42 seats is the most of any party but fewer than a majority
Yes. It won more seats than any other party
Yes. 42 seats is a majority of 88
No. Only the Plains Party can form government
qs.x: 42 is three short of 45. Harbour has the most seats but not majority support, so it cannot govern alone.

qs.q: Which arrangement would give the Plains Party majority support?
o: An agreement with the Rivers Alliance and at least two independents
A coalition with the Rivers Alliance alone
An agreement with one independent
None is needed, because 38 seats is already a majority
qs.x: 38 plus 5 is 43, still short. Adding two independents makes 45. Plains would need the Rivers Alliance and at least two of the three independents.

qs.q: The Harbour Party reaches an agreement with the three independents and forms government. Who forms the Opposition?
o: The Plains Party, the largest group not in government
The Rivers Alliance, because it is on the crossbench
The three independents, because they are not in a party
Nobody, because the Harbour Party now has majority support
qs.x: The Opposition is the largest party or coalition not in government. The Rivers Alliance sits on the crossbench, and so do the independents even though they support the government.

sources.caption: Scenario 6. A morning at the Magistrates' Court
sources.text: Situation A. A duty lawyer gives free advice to a person who cannot afford a lawyer, so they understand the charge before their hearing. Situation B. A magistrate realises she coached the accused's football team for three years and asks another magistrate to hear the case. Situation C. A well-known footballer and a shop assistant are each fined the same amount for the same parking offence. Situation D. The court in a regional town closes, so residents must now travel 300 kilometres to attend a hearing.

qs.q: Which principle of justice is strengthened in Situation A?
o: Access
Equality
Stability
Separation of powers
qs.x: Access means people can understand and use the legal system whatever their circumstances. Free advice removes a barrier for someone who cannot pay.

qs.q: In Situation B, the magistrate is protecting which principle?
o: Fairness, because a decision-maker must be impartial
Equality, because both people are treated the same
Access, because the case will be heard faster
Stability, because the law has not changed
qs.x: A personal connection could bias the decision, or make it look biased. Stepping aside keeps the process impartial, which is fairness.

qs.q: What does Situation C show?
o: Equality before the law: the law applied in the same way regardless of fame
Equity: each person received support according to need
Access: both people could reach the court
Fairness: both people were allowed to speak
qs.x: Equality means the law treats everyone the same whatever their position or status.

qs.q: Which principle is weakened in Situation D?
o: Access, because distance makes the court harder to use
Equality, because the law has changed for the town
Fairness, because the magistrate is biased
Stability, because court dates keep changing
qs.x: Having to travel 300 kilometres is a barrier to using the legal system, especially for people without transport or money. That is a loss of access.

sources.caption: Scenario 7. Becoming Australian
sources.text: Priya moved to Australia from India eight years ago. Last Saturday she made the citizenship pledge at a council ceremony. Her brother Dev was born in Australia and turned 19 last year, but he has never enrolled to vote. Their neighbour Tom says a person is not really Australian unless they were born here. Priya still celebrates Diwali with her family every year.

qs.q: What changed for Priya legally when she became a citizen?
o: She gained rights such as voting and an Australian passport, and responsibilities such as enrolling to vote
She must stop celebrating traditions from her country of birth
She automatically became a member of Parliament
Nothing changed, because she already lived in Australia
qs.x: Citizenship is formal legal membership. It brings rights, like voting and a passport, and responsibilities, like enrolling and voting. It does not change a person's culture.

qs.q: Is Dev meeting his responsibilities as a citizen?
o: No. Eligible citizens aged 18 and over must enrol and vote
Yes. Voting is optional for citizens born in Australia
Yes. Only new citizens have to enrol
No. He should have enrolled at 16, which is compulsory
qs.x: Enrolling and voting are compulsory for citizens aged 18 and over. Enrolment is possible from 16 but not compulsory until 18.

qs.q: Which statement best responds to Tom's claim?
o: National identity is shaped by many things, such as values, culture and experience, not only place of birth
Tom is right: citizenship is only possible for people born in Australia
Only people who vote can call themselves Australian
National identity and citizenship are the same thing
qs.x: Citizenship is a legal status that people gain by birth or by applying. National identity is a sense of belonging shaped by many factors.

qs.q: Which of these can Priya do as a citizen that a permanent resident cannot?
o: Vote in federal elections
Work in Australia
Attend an Australian school
Hold a Victorian driver licence
qs.x: Permanent residents can work, study and drive. Voting in federal elections, holding an Australian passport and standing for Parliament are for citizens.
